title: Triple-I and Munich Re's RiskScan 2026 Surveys 1,700 People and Finds Cyber, Economic Volatility and Catastrophe Concerns Linked, as the $424 Billion Protection Gap Persists
summary: RiskScan 2026, released on June 8 by the Insurance Information Institute and Munich Re US, surveyed more than 1,700 people in the US and UK and found risks increasingly seen as interconnected, with cyber and flood protection gaps persisting against a global natural catastrophe protection gap that Swiss Re put at $424 billion.
description:
A joint study by the Insurance Information Institute, known as Triple-I, and Munich Re US has set out how people across the insurance chain view risk in 2026, and the central result is that they no longer see threats in isolation. RiskScan 2026, released on June 8, surveyed more than 1,700 participants in the United States and the United Kingdom across five groups: consumers, small business owners, middle-market decision-makers, property and casualty agents and brokers, and P&C carriers. The study is organised into two reports, one on reinsurance exposures and one on specialty insurance. This article draws on a report by Insurance Business, and the survey is a snapshot of opinion, not a measurement of losses.

Risks seen as connected

Respondents flagged cyber incidents, economic volatility, natural catastrophes, artificial intelligence, business interruption and emerging liability exposures as top concerns. The notable point is that they tended to view these as linked, not separate. A cyber incident can cause business interruption; an economic shock can change a firm's ability to invest in resilience; a catastrophe can disrupt systems that then fail in other ways. Triple-I chief economist Michel Léonard said economic conditions are a multiplier of insurance risk, affecting affordability, claims severity and capital allocation.

The study also reports a shift in thinking about catastrophes. Floods, severe storms, winter weather and wildfires, which are not the headline peak perils such as major hurricanes and earthquakes, are now seen as frequent and high-impact. That challenges long-held views about catastrophe exposure and about how diversified an insurer's portfolio is, because a series of mid-sized events can add up.

The protection gap

The study cites Swiss Re's sigma report, published days earlier, which put the global natural catastrophe protection gap at $424 billion. The protection gap is the part of economic losses that is not covered by insurance. In North America, the insurance coverage ratio has stayed between 40% and 42% since 2015, according to the study, which means a majority of catastrophe losses are still borne by uninsured individuals and businesses. The report does not analyse why the ratio has not moved.

The specialty report found that cyber and flood protection gaps are persisting and widening. Newfront's head of cyber, Jennifer Wilson, said inconsistent policy language across insurers complicates coverage decisions. When policy wordings differ in how they treat the same event, a buyer may not know whether a loss would be covered until a claim is made.

Legal costs

Respondents increasingly see legal system abuse as a driver of rising P&C costs. The term refers to litigation practices that raise claim costs, such as inflated claims or tactics that add expense. The report does not provide measurements of the effect so the finding should be read as the perception of the survey groups.

Artificial intelligence

AI ranked as the most impactful emerging technology across all five segments. HSB, which is part of Munich Re, found that 74% of small businesses already use AI tools. HSB's Timothy Zeilman said AI risk resembles early cyber risk, largely hidden in traditional policies until losses forced attention. That comparison suggests that insurers may face a period in which AI-related losses are not clearly assigned to any policy, until wordings are clarified or exclusions are introduced. It is an analogy, not a forecast.

Quotes and calls for collaboration

Marcus Winter of Munich Re US stressed the role of insurance in community recovery and resilience. Triple-I chief executive Sean Kevelighan said recognising risk is only the first step and called for collaboration across the industry, policymakers and communities. The study is therefore also an advocacy document, which is typical of industry research and is worth bearing in mind when interpreting its recommendations.

Reading the results as a map of risk

It helps to treat the survey as a map showing where insurers and their customers agree and disagree. They agree that cyber, catastrophe and economic risk are all important. The less comfortable finding is that protection gaps in cyber and flood are widening even though awareness is high. Awareness does not automatically lead to purchases, and the report points to inconsistent policy language as one reason. That suggests that clearer, more standard wordings, or better explanation by brokers, could narrow the gap, although the summary does not test that idea.

The combination of AI and cyber is another theme. Respondents ranked AI as the most impactful emerging technology, while cyber incidents topped concerns, and the study's specialty report links the two by noting that AI can make attacks more sophisticated and underwriting less certain. That link comes from the report's own framing, and the figures here do not measure how much AI has changed cyber losses.

Limits of the survey

The survey covers the United States and the United Kingdom, so its findings may not apply elsewhere. The report does not give the size of each group or the percentage breakdown of the answers in the summary, so the weight of each concern cannot be assessed. The Insurance Business summary also does not give the date range of fieldwork.

What to do with it

For businesses, the study is a prompt to review how cyber, flood and business interruption cover interact and to ask whether policy wordings are consistent. For insurers, it highlights where customers and carriers see gaps. For policymakers, the persistent protection gap supports arguments for risk reduction and resilience investment. This article summarises a trade-press report of an industry study and is general information, not insurance advice.
source_name: Insurance Business, reporting Triple-I and Munich Re US RiskScan 2026 (June 2026)
image_alt: Global insurance risk analysis and protection gap research (illustrative)
key_points: RiskScan 2026 surveyed more than 1,700 participants in the US and UK across five groups: consumers, small business owners, middle-market decision-makers, property and casualty agents and brokers, and P&C carriers.
Respondents flagged cyber incidents, economic volatility, natural catastrophes, AI, business interruption and emerging liability exposures, and tended to see them as linked rather than separate.
Swiss Re's sigma report, published days earlier, put the global natural catastrophe protection gap at $424 billion, and North America's coverage ratio has stayed between 40% and 42% since 2015.
The specialty report found cyber and flood protection gaps persisting and widening, and respondents increasingly see legal system abuse as a driver of rising P&C costs.
AI ranked as the most impactful emerging technology in all segments, and HSB found 74% of small businesses already use AI tools.
why_it_matters: Surveys of insurers and their customers show whether the two sides see risk the same way. The finding that risks are seen as overlapping, and that cyber and flood cover remain patchy, points to where uninsured losses are most likely to land.

title: The Fidelis Partnership Launches a Lloyd's PVT Consortium With Up to $47.5 Million Per Risk in the Middle East as War-Risk Demand Rises
summary: The Fidelis Partnership launched the TFP PVT Consortium in early June 2026, bringing together Lloyd's syndicates including Argenta and TFP's own, backed by Pelagos and placed by Guy Carpenter, with up to $47.5 million per risk in the Middle East and $345 million elsewhere.
description:
Capacity for war, terrorism and political violence insurance is scarce, and a group of Lloyd's insurers has launched a consortium to supply more of it. The Fidelis Partnership (TFP) launched the TFP PVT Consortium in early June 2026, according to a report by Insurance Business on June 5, 2026. The consortium deploys capacity into what the market calls the WTPV market, where demand is rising and supply is tightening after the Middle East conflict. This article summarises that report. An earlier version of this article described the consortium as a Lloyd's of London initiative. The report describes it as a TFP-led consortium of Lloyd's syndicates, not an initiative of the Lloyd's corporation itself, and the headline has been corrected.

Who is in the consortium? Members include several Lloyd's syndicates, among them Argenta, and TFP's own Syndicates 3123 and 2126. Guy Carpenter placed the consortium, meaning that the broker arranged it with the capacity providers. Pelagos Insurance Capital is the cornerstone capacity provider, which means that it supplies the anchor support on which the consortium is built. A consortium in this context is a group of insurers that agree to write a risk together under a lead underwriter, so the buyer can place a large limit through a single process and not many separate negotiations.

How much cover is available? The consortium can provide up to $47.5 million per risk in the Middle East and up to $345 million per risk in other global markets, according to the report. The lower limit for the Middle East reflects the greater uncertainty and accumulation concerns there. The report does not say what types of property or business the consortium targets, or how premiums are set.

What is the market context? The article cites average political violence rate increases of 15% to 25% through 2026 and says aggregate limits are tightening by 10% to 15% year over year. Aggregate limits are the maximum an insurer will pay in total over a policy period, so tightening means buyers get less total protection. Together with price increases, that makes cover harder and more expensive to obtain. Separate reporting on this site describes how marine war-risk premiums for ships in the Strait of Hormuz rose sharply, and how a government-backed facility was set up to supply capacity. The consortium focuses on a different part of the market, political violence insurance for property and business operations on land.

What did the executives say? Billy Ayres, head of underwriting for crisis management at TFP, called the launch a direct expression of the firm's high-conviction approach, and said the consortium gives clients certainty at the moment they need it most. Darren Hines, unit head of terrorism at Argenta, said it arrives at a critical point for buyers seeking dependable capacity, and that the structure brings together strong underwriting leadership and meaningful capacity. Jonathan Powell, managing director at Guy Carpenter, said clients are facing urgent and complex capacity needs following the Middle East conflict. These statements come from the people and firms involved and are promotional in tone.

What does it mean for buyers? Companies with operations or assets in the Middle East and other conflict-prone regions may find that more capacity is available through consortium arrangements, but at higher prices and with tighter terms. Buyers should expect insurers to scrutinise accumulations of risk, which is the concentration of insured assets in a single location. They should discuss with brokers how much cover they need, and whether a combination of lines such as property, political violence and trade credit is appropriate. The report does not give prices.

What does it mean for the market? New capacity can help moderate price rises and relieve strain. At the same time, the softening cycle in other specialty lines, covered in WTW's survey and Lloyd's own results elsewhere on this site, shows that capital moves quickly to where returns look attractive. War and political violence are an exception because of the geopolitical situation, and the extent of new entrants such as consortiums will determine whether the tightness persists.

How does Lloyd's fit in? Lloyd's is the marketplace in which the syndicates operate, and syndicates are managed by managing agents that decide what risks to write. TFP's own syndicates are part of that structure.

What are the limits of the information? The report does not state the consortium's total size, the shares of each member, or the exact scope of cover. It does not say whether it will write cover for ships, which is typically handled in the marine war market, or whether it focuses on land-based assets. It also does not say how much of the capacity is already deployed. For these reasons, readers should treat the headline limits as the maximum available to the consortium for a single risk, not as a measure of how much cover will actually be bought.

Why are limits lower in the Middle East? Underwriters set lower maximums where the probability of loss is higher or where several insured assets could be hit by the same event. A $47.5 million limit per risk compared with $345 million elsewhere reflects that caution. Buyers in the region needing larger limits would have to build programmes from several markets.

This article summarises a trade report and is not insurance advice.
source_name: Insurance Business (June 5, 2026), Global Reinsurance and Bernews

Members include several Lloyd's syndicates, among them Argenta and TFP's own Syndicates 3123 and 2126; Guy Carpenter placed the consortium and Pelagos Insurance Capital is the cornerstone capacity provider.
Capacity is up to $47.5 million per risk in the Middle East and up to $345 million per risk in other global markets.
The article cites average political violence rate increases of 15% to 25% through 2026 and aggregate limits tightening by 10% to 15% year over year.
Executives say the consortium gives clients certainty when they need it most; Guy Carpenter's Jonathan Powell says clients face urgent and complex capacity needs after the Middle East conflict.
why_it_matters: War, terrorism and political violence cover protects businesses with assets in unstable regions. When insurers pull back, consortiums that combine capacity can keep cover available, though prices and limits are tight.
